utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Monday, the 16th of February, 2009. I'd like to greet Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Pusic, as well as all the lawyers, counsel, the OTP in its entirety, as well as all the people assisting us in this courtroom. I believe that the registrar has a few IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Buljan Stijepo. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC 921. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC 922, the list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC 923, and the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC 924. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, the Trial Chamber is going to ask you to clarify the following: The Prosecutor filed a motion regarding the witness of today, as well as the exhibits that will be shown. The Prosecution claims all of this is tu quoque. Let me remind you that as far as Witness Beese is concerned, pursuant the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the principle of tu quoque does not apply to humanitarian law, insofar as the obligation under this law are designed to protect fundamental human values and should be abided by, by all the parties, notwithstanding the behaviour of all the other party or parties. The Trial Chamber had decided that considering, therefore, that the evidence presented with the sole purpose of claiming tu quoque would be irrelevant and should therefore not be admitted. But there was another point of the decision that said considering that evidence relating to the atrocities committed against the Croats in Bosnia could only be admitted if the latter would challenge one of the allegations mentioned in the indictment. Ms. Nozica, you have read the motion of the Prosecution. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everybody else in the courtroom. Yes, I have seen the Prosecution motion, and I'd like to say at the outset that the Defence of Bruno Stojic is not going to use the tu quoque defence, but would like, through this witness, who was otherwise in charge of providing information to the public, as well as to the HVO internally, has certain direct knowledge about certain events which took place in the material period in HZ-HB. Now, in the courtroom we've had quite a lot of discussion on documents and issues which show the suffering of the Croats and the crimes committed against the Croats, and we considered -- or, rather, the Defence considers that those events and those documents are important for the general context in which the events occurred in Herceg-Bosna, and therefore we consider that the objection made by the Prosecutor is premature. And the list we provided of witnesses, and we have provided it on time and quite a lot in advance, before we bring the witness in, suddenly we're faced with this motion from the Prosecution, their objection. All that I can say in that regard is, as His Honour Judge Antonetti just said, some of those -- that evidence need not be relevant and therefore tendered and admitted into evidence. I would like to present some of those documents, because as I say, I think they are significant, in view of the information that this witness can provide us with, and it is up to the Trial Chamber ultimately. If the Prosecution objects, to decide whether they are indeed relevant and whether they will be admitted into evidence or not. Because when we come to tender exhibits and documents, it is always the Trial Chamber that makes the final decision. So that's what I can say in that regard at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, to clarify things even better: As far as Trusina is concerned, 2D 00815 and 2D 157, what is it you wish to prove by putting questions to the witness about Trusina?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this witness received -- well, I'm not going to say what my case is and what I wish to prove, but I want to say that the witness had information and received information, and then he can tell us which information he received about that particular matter. The event relevant to Trusina is very important. It took place on the 16th of April, 1993, and so it is highly significant, also with respect to all the other events that took place in April in the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO. Now, I don't wish to testify on the subject, nor to provide any closing arguments, but I think that it will be very difficult for the Trial Chamber to reach a conclusion as to what actually happened if it makes it impossible for the Defence to focus on events which relate to the activities of the BH Army, including the crimes that were committed of the. May I just finish and say that I wish to emphasise, and this will be seen from this witness's testimony as well, that the month of April, April 1993, is an exceptionally important month, both from the aspects of the indictment and the aspects of the evidence and exhibits put forward by the Defence and also by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I might ask a question. As far as the relevance of exhibits relating to Trusina are concerned, in what way is it relevant to say that in that Croatian village, on the 16th of April, 1993, Croats were slaughtered or massacred? In what way is it relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I consider this to be exceptionally relevant with respect to the indictment, because I consider that those events, and I said this a moment ago, are linked to all the events that took place in the month of April, and I think it's very relevant to throw light on the way in which the BH Army acted under the circumstances, and especially the 4th Corps. We're dealing with the activities of the 4th Corps, in actual fact, so that entire area is one we have to look at. And I remember full well something that Mr. Praljak said -- General Praljak said on one occasion, and I fully support him. You can't extract events and place them in a vacuum. Events happened as was presented by the Prosecutor, but they took place in a way in which the Defence presented it, so it's up to the Court to show how far they affected some future events. But I'd like to suggest to the Trial Chamber, in view of some of the documents presented thus far in the courtroom and are linked to the name of this particular witness, that the Trial Chamber will precisely look at the events of the 15th, 16th, and 17th, and 18th of April, and only once it has done that, all the days around the 16th of April, will it be able to weigh up the evidence and create a picture for itself. It's very difficult for me to say anything that would avoid me testifying. However, I also do wish to stress that it is very difficult to understand the events in Mostar, for example, if we're talking about the events of the 9th of May onwards, and even the events of April, the 25th of April onwards, if we don't link that up to the events in Jablanica, Konjic and Trusina, is precisely in that area. So it's impossible to separate these events, to separate one segment of that area, without looking at the whole area and what was happening in that area. So, Your Honours, if that suffices, then I have finished. If not, I shall be happy to provide additional information. I'd just like to emphasise -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: But if you didn't finish, please kindly do so. And afterwards, I will speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more sentence, and it's this: We did have an opportunity of seeing here a report by UNPROFOR and the other international organisations which spoke about these events, and those documents were admitted into evidence. They are in exhibits, and they related to that. Well, that's what I wanted to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I, of course, fully agree with what our President has said and also asked questions concerning the submission of the Prosecution and, of course, the Defence position on certain documents. I would only like to clarify one particular issue, and it is merely the very principle which is called as shorthand "tu quoque," but as a matter of fact it has its official name as a principle, and I quote, which is also contained in the volume of the Customary International Law -- International Humanitarian Law published by the ICRC and in the preparation of which I had some very modest role, but my point is here that this issue, which is called, in general, "tu quoque," is being submitted as - and I quote: "The obligation to respect and ensure respect for international humanitarian law does not depend on reciprocity." And I would like to recall that principle, which again I say has also a kind of number 140, and the authors of the book, the publication, refer, among others, also to the work of the ICTY on that matter, and also the decision of the International Court of Justice in the Namibia case in 1971, and when they speak about the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, the Kupreskic case, which was also mentioned by the Prosecution submission, and also the Matic case in 1996. So my point is, what I would like to make, is this principle has been generally adopted and also always mentioned as an obligation to respect the rules of International Humanitarian Law, without referring to any dependence on reciprocity, so it was my point. And I would like to say that, of course, on individual cases the Chamber will deliberate and then to make its own decision as it sees proper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to make the following comment: I did not take part in the drafting of any such laws as has Judge Prandler, but as far as I am concerned, tu quoque cannot be supported to allege non-guilt, pursuant to 7.1 and 7.3, those two Articles of the Statute, but can be presented to the opposing party to enable Judges to understand the spirit in which one of the parties to the conflict found itself when the latter party discovered that so many people had been killed. This is the third bullet point of the decision we handed down. This is what I wanted to say to make sure that all of this is very clear. As far as I'm concerned, the Defence teams can put the questions to the witness and say as follows: "How come there were these massacres in Trusina? Since you were in charge of propaganda and information, what was the state of mind of the soldiers, of the international community?" Such questions can be asked, but this cannot disprove the criminal guilt of anyone. We are wasting time with this motion, because the Stojic Defence team goes into long arguments and the Bench has to intervene. What a waste of time. But my colleague is about to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Scott. I am quite aware you have been waiting for the floor, but I have two questions to address to you which you might then perhaps address in the same time. The first question is: What is the relevance of your objection? Is it something else than the will to avoid losing time? And the second point is: To what extent does the Prosecution contest the facts that the Defence wants to establish with regard to these villages and the behaviour of ABiH? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Judge Trechsel. All of Your Honours, good afternoon to all of you. Good afternoon to counsel, everyone in the courtroom. If I could just have two minutes, Your Honour, to summarise our position and respond to Judge Trechsel's questions. It's unfortunate it's perceived that the motion is a waste of time. Of course, the Prosecution doesn't file motions that it thinks are wasting time. We've looked ahead, and not only with this witness but with the upcoming -- some of the upcoming Stojic material, and it just -- it appears to us, and I emphasise the word "appears," it appears to us that over the next weeks we may be spending potentially a lot of time on things that the Prosecution considers involves tu quoque or very close to tu quoque, and therefore we think it is entirely right and proper for the Prosecution to raise its concerns. We've all said -- everyone in this courtroom has said just recently, this is a long trial. It will only be made that much longer by taking the courtroom time to deal with irrelevant issues which are not Defences and which only take time. The Chamber has ruled before that -- this proper scope and has specifically required in its previous ruling, that before counsel can put a question or put a document to the witness that touches on the tu quoque concept, that there must be an articulated basis for doing so other than tu quoque itself. And that's the Chamber's ruling. That's not the Prosecution's ruling; that's the ruling that the Chamber has adopted, and it appeared to us appropriate to remind everyone in the courtroom of that ruling on that point. So, Your Honours, we will certainly listen to the Defence questions and the answers, and we will also expect, of course, counsel to abide by the Trial Chamber's rulings, that prior to putting any question touching on this or using any exhibit, that they will articulate a separate basis for doing so. So of course we'll expect that to happen. To answer your questions, Judge Trechsel: As we've said many times, I believe as I said in the opening statement some years ago, we -- the Prosecution has never disputed that there are -- there were crimes and atrocities committed against Croat victims by Muslims. As you all know by now, this Tribunal knows full well that there were perpetrators on all sides, if you will, and victims on all sides, each of them to be -- each of the perpetrators to be equally condemned, each of the victims to be equally sympathised with. But the fact of the matter is this is the case that we're in now, and the fact that the crimes were committed on the other side, Your Honour, is not a Defence, and we do think has the potential to take an awful lot of courtroom time for dealing with things that are not relevant. There is also, and I say this -- I'm trying to give as neutral a word as possible. I'm not accusing the Defence of bad faith. Let me make that very clear. What I'm about to say has nothing to do with bad faith. But having said that, there is the potential for a lot of courtroom misdirection and consumption of time on matters that are not truly at issue or relevant, and therefore once again, Your Honours, it appeared to us entirely appropriate to raise our concerns with the Chamber and to bring perhaps back on the screen, if you will, of everyone in the courtroom concerning these matters. I think that states where we are, Your Honours, and we'll go forward on that basis, and if the Prosecution believes that a particular question and answer are not appropriate on this basis, then of course I will rise to my feet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, after having deliberated, has noted the motion filed by the Prosecution, the explanations provided by Ms. Nozica, has also acknowledged the position of the Prosecution, who has just said that he will listen carefully to the questions that are put and may, if need be, intervene. The Trial Chamber would like to remind Ms. Nozica that we did hand down a decision and that we would like her, as regards this particular decision, to be extremely careful and only put questions that are strictly necessary to her case. The Trial Chamber is unanimous in saying that tu quoque is part of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and is not a way of exonerating the criminal responsibility of a perpetrator. Ms. Nozica, you can show your documents, but make sure you focus on your questions. From what I understood, Mr. Karnavas wanted to say something. If he would like to, I would like him to be short. Otherwise, we'll bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I did wish to make some oral submissions concerning my client, especially given that I've been given instructions to do so at this point in time. As you know, Mr. Prlic -- Dr. Prlic is not here with us, although he was in court throughout the entire Prosecution case and throughout the entire part of his case. After long deliberations and consultation and research that we've done, Dr. Prlic has come to the conclusion that at this point in time, he wishes to waive his right to be present in court. He understands that this is a -- this is not an unqualified right, that he can in fact waive it, just as he waived his right to an expeditious trial. He's waiving his right to be present. And if I would -- if I could make reference to the Milosevic case just very briefly. If you might remember, in that instance where Mr. Milosevic wanted to represent himself, but was ill at some point in time, the Appeals Chamber in fact has left the door open that even if, for instance, an accused wishes to be present but is unable to be present, the Trial Chamber can go forward nonetheless with the trial. In other words, it would appear that the jurisprudence is going in the direction where trials in absentia are, in fact, permissible in the -- at this particular tribunal and in international criminal law, and I also point out that that is exactly what is envisaged in Article 22 of the Statute of the Special Tribunal for Lebanon. As we all know, it was President Cassese -- Professor Cassese who was going -- at least goes around saying he's going to be the next president of that -- or the first president of that tribunal. He drafted the Statute, and Article 22 of that Statute provides for trials in absentia when the accused need not be present in court while the trial is going on, provided, of course, certain conditions are met. And that leads me to my next point, which I was specifically given instructions to raise at this time. It is our -- it is Dr. Prlic's intention to file a motion for provisional release for the remainder of the trial. He does so on a number of grounds. We will be filing a written motion, but nonetheless I was instructed to briefly, within two or three minutes, outline the reasons for that. One. As we all know, he still enjoys and will continue to enjoy the presumption of innocence, and that is something that is steeped into the Tribunal Statute, Article 21(3) as well, which is also based on, as we all know, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Now, the procedure at this particular Tribunal under Rule 65(a) does not prohibit -- the way we read it, does not prohibit provisional release during the trial, provided an accused waives his presence. In fact, when it was -- when that particular Rule was amended back in July 2000, the notion that exceptional circumstances was a precondition for provisional release was taken out of the Rule. Also, if you -- as you all well know, the report of experts -- the report of the expert group that conducted a review at the ICTY into seeing how it could become more efficient, both at the ICTY and ICTR, also recommended that an accused be granted provisional release provided that they are waiving their presence, and this would go into, at the trial stage, if they met three criteria: they freely and knowingly waived their right; the personal circumstances in favour for provisional release. In this instance, we will be getting security guarantees from Croatia; and the guarantee by counsel that they are willing to participate in the trial in absentia, and of course we are willing to remain in the course -- in the case and proceed, as we have, throughout the course of these proceedings. The trial is taking an unreasonably long period of time to be completed, and that's the nature of this particular -- this particular case, based on the indictment, and therefore based -- that is one other reason why we believe that Dr. Prlic need not be in custody, because custody, pre-trial, or trial custody is not a form of punishment, it's not a form of punishment. And I might bring to the Trial Chamber's attention, in the Blagojevic/Jokic case, prior to the trial Judge Schomburg had even issued that Mr. Jokic be provisionally released throughout the trial while in The Hague, and it was the Netherlands that kicked up a fuss because part of their agreement with the ICTY and the UN is that all accused, while in The Hague, will be residing at the UNDU unless other circumstances are made -- other considerations are put in place, such as the Blaskic case. As we all know he was put under house arrest initially. Finally, and we do take note of the fact, for instance, that in the Appeals Chamber recently, in denying the provisional release of two of the accused in this particular case, has indicated that one must demonstrate sufficiently compelling humanitarian reasons, although I would -- I dare say -- I dare say that the dissenting opinion in that case is much more in line with the law, and that this notion that somehow sufficiently compelling humanitarian reasons must exist is something that does not exist in customary international law; it is something that is simply, for lack of a better phrase, was made up by the Appeals Chamber. And perhaps that may be the reason for provisional release during a recess. We're saying in this instance this is not a recess. Dr. Prlic, above and beyond all the reasons I've stated, wishes to be provisionally released in order that he can participate more, not less, in his defence, and it is our belief that he can participate more if, for instance, he has access to a computer and to internet while the proceedings are going on. He can communicate through counsel as we normally do with our legal assistants and our case managers, who are only situated a floor from here. He can provide just as much of assistance to us. And as you may recall, he initially he had made a request to have a computer present in court so he could type out his thoughts and his notes and provide them to us, and it has been a monumental task for us to be able to get his input into this case. I know it doesn't sound like much to those sitting on the Bench or to those who work for Chambers, but for counsel to have to go every day to the UNDU to get a disc that has been downloaded and burned, and get through with the paperwork, and we do this almost on a constant day-to-day basis, and so for all of these reasons Dr. Prlic will be filing a motion for provisional release for the remainder of the period. And I just want to make it very, very clear to the Trial Chamber Dr. Prlic remains profoundly engaged in this trial, he remains profoundly in respect of this Trial Chamber, and wishes to continue to participate in any form. It's just that he believes that: one, he need not be in this courtroom at the time and he can participate more effectively out of court; and, two, because of the length of the case, he feels it is better for his physical and mental health if he is not incarcerated, as he is now, and that he be allowed to participate in absentia while provisionally released. These were the submission that I was asked to make. I appreciate the Court's time. I know we're under some tight time limitations, but nonetheless I wanted to make sure the Trial Chamber understood that his absence should not be taken in any form as disrespect to the members of this Trial Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very well, thank you. We are expecting the filing from the Prlic Defence counsel and from the Prosecution as well, and then we shall decide. Thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas, for having informing us that President Cassese would preside over the Court for Lebanon. This is a scoop. Thank you very much for this. Now, we are going to show the witness in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us your name, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Veso Vegar. 11th of September, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what newspaper do you work as a journalist? I'm asking you questions from the English text, because I cannot hear the French booth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired. I no longer work as a journalist right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're retired. Now, did you already come to court as a witness or do you come here for the first time in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would please ask you to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated. Some information for you, but I think that Ms. Nozica has probably given you this information when she met with you before the hearing. You are going to answer questions from Ms. Nozica, also on the basis of the documents, most likely. Now, once this is done, the other lawyers of the -- counsels of the other accused shall also ask you questions during their cross-examination. Then the Prosecutor, sitting to your right, will have the same amount of time as Ms. Nozica to ask you questions during his cross-examination. The four Judges sitting before you may also, if the case arises, ask you questions. Well, as a rule, we ask you questions from the documents, because we see that there is a document and some points of clarification must be brought, and so we ask you questions about that in order to highlight the above-mentioned document. Now, you are a witness in this court of justice. So you do not belong to Ms. Nozica. You've taken the oath, which means that for the next few days you shall have no contact with anybody, of course, except with members of your family, but no contacts with the press, no contacts with anyone, X, Y, Z, in order to explain how things are going here in court. We shall take breaks every hour and a half, 20-minute breaks, but if you feel tired or if there is a problem, please raise your right hand, in which case we shall make a break for you to take a rest. So this is what I wanted to say by way of introduction to make sure that proceedings go smoothly. This is your first time here as a witness, and you will realise that it is very tiring. You will answer questions, and in the course of time the witness can get tired. But in spite of that, I would like to ask you to be as precise and accurate as you can, because the Judges will be able to draw conclusions on the basis of your replies. So this is, sir, what I wanted to tell you, and without further adieu I would like to hand over the floor to Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet you, Mr. Vegar. We are going to broach certain questions concerning your CV, curriculum vitae. I'd like to be as brief as possible, and you will assist me, of course, in certain areas. I hope that leading questions will be tolerated so that we can go through this phase as quickly as possible. Mr. Vegar, you were born in the village of Vacerovici [phoen], Ljubuski municipality; am I right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will briefly go through the details that you provided, until the point that you were involved in HZ-HB. You graduated from Political Science School in Sarajevo in 1981; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Department of Journalism; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Your first job was in the public university at Ljubuski in 1983; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From 1987 until 1989, you worked at a company in the town of Ploce; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From 1989 to 1990, you were a journalist, weren't you, correspondent for "Vecernji List," a Zagreb-based newspaper?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: "Vecernji List" and then Radio Split and Radio Zagreb afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you at the same time were a journalist -- a correspondent of Radio Split and Radio Zagreb; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In September 1992, you were appointed as head of Information and Administration -- information and propaganda --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that the lawyer would ask you what was the nature of your work as a journalist, so we know that you worked in -- you were a journalist in a newspaper, then in Radio Split and Zagreb. What was your scope of competence? Did you work in sports, or were you specialised in politics, in economics? What exactly was your expertise, or were you a journalist working on general issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I covered all issues; politics, economy, and sometimes sports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were a mainstream journalist, sort of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is how correspondents work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We've come to September 1992. Could you please tell us what happened in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: At that time, as we know, the war had broken out in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was appointed as head of the Administration for Information and Propaganda in the Defence Department of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Which sector?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: The moral upbringing sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who was assistant head of the Defence Department for moral upbringing sector?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Mr. Bozo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did Bozo Rajic leave at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: At the end of 1992 or at the beginning of 1993, Bozo Rajic assumed another post as minister of defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, who and when proposed that you be appointed as assistant head for -- although this sector used to be labelled "Moral Upbringing Sector" and later on was the Sector for Information and Propaganda Activities, was it not, Mr. Vegar? But won't we use the henceforth acronym IPD?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who proposed that you be appointed there and when, to be appointed as assistant head for IPD?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Assistant head, Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you recall when?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: 31st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber when were you officially appointed and by whom?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: I was officially appointed by the HVO HZ-HB. I received the decision in August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you explain when you left that position?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: I left it after the new composition of the Croatian Defence Council was created, the end of -- but I remained there until the 30th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you gain employment again at Slobodna Dalmacija in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Slobodna Dalmacija?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, did you, at the beginning of 1997, you gain employment in the Federal Defence Ministry of the Federation BiH at Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Which position did you fulfill and until when?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Assistant defence minister. I stayed there until the middle of the following year, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: After that, I worked in the Republic of Croatia Embassy in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Which post?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: The first secretary in charge of culture.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Until when did you remain there, and what was your next post?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: I stayed there for two years, and after that I worked in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was it 2000? Could you explain your position within the Presidency office?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes, that was 2000 that I worked as an adviser to the Croatian member of the Presidency, Mr. Jelavic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was your purview?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Primarily culture and education.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you, in April 2001, you establish your own company?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You worked there until 2003; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In 2003, you went to another company, where you worked as a manager?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you retired on the 27th of December, 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that you worked on tasks concerning information and propaganda, it would be meaningful for me to ask you whether you have ever been a member of the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, a party that was predominantly peopled by Croats?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: If you mean the BiH, then my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, out of curiosity, I heard very carefully the way in which you described your career, which is extremely diversified and very interesting, and I realised that you were first a secretary of the Embassy of the Republic of Croatia in Sarajevo. Does that mean that you have two citizenships, that you're a Croat, which would explain why you were a first secretary with the embassy, and are you also a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have dual citizenship of both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have two passports, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am entitled to two passports, but I own only the Croatian passport because it allows for easier travel abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, you were asked whether you were ever a member of the HVO, and you did not answer by "yes" or "no," but you said, "Of BiH, no." That leaves the possibility open that you were in some other way a member of HVO. Could you -- or HZ. Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I was not a member of the political party HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, but I was a member of the HVO. I was first a soldier and an officer there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript refers to the HDZ. This is the title of the political party, and this is how I understood the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But since there were questions raised in this courtroom about the dual citizenship, both Croatian and BiH, I will ask you whether the Croatian Constitution allows for dual citizenship.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is there a prescribed procedure for acquiring Croatian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Most probably so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Most probably, since you gained citizenship using that procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said another interesting thing that should be explained to the Trial Chamber. You say that, "I own just the Croatian passport because it provides for easier travel." Could you explain to the Trial Chamber the advantage of a Croatian passport over a Bosnian and Herzegovinian passport at this point and in the period from 1997 onwards? Do you need visas to visit certain countries of the Schengen Agreement?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: No, this is the huge advantage of the Croatian passport. Had I used the BH passport, I would have had to wait for days in queuing for visas at embassies in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So let us be precise. Citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who have solely Bosnia-Herzegovina citizenship must acquire visas for almost all countries in Europe; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: For a majority of countries, except for Croatia and some other countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vegar, do you know whether a large number of Bosniaks and Serbs -- or don't let me suggest that there is a larger number, but do you know people who received Croatian passports using the same procedure as you did; they have Croatian citizenship and Croatian passports today?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: I do know some people of other ethnic background who received a Croatian passport before I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to the September 1992 period. You said that you were appointed as head of the IPD administration, in the moral upbringing sector. You said that you were proposed for the post of assistant head of the Defence Department on the 31st of January 1993. Please tell us, what were your tasks as head of the IPD administration in the period from September 1993 -- correction, in September 1992 until 31st of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: My primary task was to disseminate information, first collect them from all available sources, to analyse such information, systematise them and then disseminate them. There were two forms: Internal information dissemination within military units and external dissemination of information towards the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court the way in which you gathered information from your position as head of the IPD? Where did you get the information from?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: The information came in from the assistant for IPDs or, rather, assistants, where they existed in the HVO structure, and also from the Main Staff, and from the Defence Department as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you collected all the information, and you said that they were used for internal information and for dissemination to the information media, it emerges that on the 31st of January, 1993, from the information you've given us, you were put forward by Mr. Stojic to be the assistant head of the Defence Department for Information and Propaganda. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how that sector was set up? What did it comprise? What made up the sector, generally.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: It was a sector within the frameworks of the Defence Department, and it had three administrations: The administration for information and propaganda; for military, psychology and social activities; and culture, sport, and recreation, and a spiritual section too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: After the 31st of January, 1993, and you said that you were officially appointed in August to that post, immediately after the 31st of January, 1993, did you in fact take over the work that an assistant head of the Defence Department for IPD would be doing?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes. After Mr. Bozo Rajic left, I did take over that job, and I also dealt with matters concerning the IPD, which was the department I worked for up until then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you continued your work in the field or, rather, in the Department for Information and Propaganda, the IPD, and the dissemination of that information and collecting information, first of all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you were the head of the entire sector, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber where the headquarters of the IPD sector was, let's say from September 1992 onwards until November 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: It was in the same building where the Main Staff was located and where the Defence Department was, and all that in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you explain a little more fully, if you know what the building was called? Do you know the name of the building, what it was called?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: It was called the Tobacco Institute of Mostar or the Apro Building.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Are you talking about September 1992 now?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Now, how long did you remain in that building, and did you remain in the building throughout, and can you tell us where the IPD sector was located afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: In the summer of 1993, because of the shelling from the enemy, the Defence Department left the building because it was a prominent building, and we went into another building into an office which was safer and secure, but also in Mostar, because the previous building was exposed to shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you stay in that building until the end of your work in the IPD or did you move on somewhere else? Did you relocate again?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: No, we didn't stay there the whole time. We relocated, and later on I went to Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, when did you go to Posusje or the office? We're talking about the office, not only you personally; right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that was at the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, at this juncture I need to express my main concern, my main question. The IPD, Information/Propaganda, you know, I find it hard to grasp what it is that you were doing there. So maybe the Defence counsel will go deeper into this field on the basis of the document, but at this juncture I'm wondering whether you were some kind of a political commissioner, or whether you were a person who was dealing with information, or someone who was involved in propaganda as part of the psychological war and a way whereby false information is disseminated in order to put the enemy in a difficult situation. So I must confess I don't know at all what it is you were doing. You know, in the Western armies, this is not something that exists. There are people in the military who are involved in information, but they are not involved in propaganda. Propaganda is more in the hands of the secret services, you see. So I'm at a loss here and I don't know what you were doing, but I'm sure that Ms. Nozica, through her questions, will lead us to and know and have a clearer picture on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour, with your permission, and that is the purpose of my examination, to gain a very clear picture of what he did. So he'll be answering all your questions, all of the questions you've just put to him, but I'd just like to ask some technical questions to gain a broader picture, and then we'll go from the broader to the narrow picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Witness, in mid-1993, right up until the end of Mr. Bruno Stojic's stay in the Defence Department as the head, you were dislocated, that is to say, you weren't in the same building where the Defence Department was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, Mr. Vegar, after that September 1992, and looking at that entire period, how many people, roughly, were employed in that IPD sector? And we saw that it had three administrations, so how many people worked there?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Four or five.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now tell me whether, in the HVO units, there were individuals who were in charge of information and propaganda.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes. This is sector also had its people in the units and at the level of the operative zones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I think there is a problem. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. It's like this: Could the witness answer this question. Is it information and propaganda or information and psychological activities? What was the name of that department or sector? And I'd like to have the witness answer that, because something that is not quite right keeps prevailing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd like to thank Mr. Praljak for that information, but the sector had a number of names, it was called in different ways, so I'd like to have the witness explain what the sector did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In some documents, it's mentioned as the Information and Propaganda Department, some where it's the Political and Propaganda, then we have Moral Guidance or Upbringing. So these terms are used in different documents, referring to the same sector, so perhaps it would be best if the witness told us what they did in that sector, because the titles and headings were different and differed. But if the witness wants to answer Mr. Praljak's question, he can go ahead, but I think that he'll best answer that question if he tells us what they, in fact, did do.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Well, officially the sector was called the Sector for Moral Guidance, but colloquially it was referred to as the IPD, Information and Psychological Activity. That was also the title. Some people thought that "IPD" was Information and Psychology, others thought it was "IP," information and Propaganda. But from the work itself, we could see that the Administration for Military Psychology was in charge of psychological activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we correct the transcript, because that was Mr. Vegar's answer on page 30, line 22, not Mr. Ibrisimovic, as it says in the transcript, but I'm sure that will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vegar, let's move on. You started telling us about the levels at which the HVO units had people working in IPD, so can you repeat that for us once again, please?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes. Within the HVO structure and the operative zone, we were supposed to have three working in IPD and also at the level of the brigades and battalions, whereas some independent companies just had one, one man working in IPD.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of your activities, and you explained to us at the beginning that you mostly dealt with collecting information for internal information purposes and also to disseminate information for the public, now, would you please tell me, from 1992, September 1992, in fact, onwards, how did you come by your information so that you could disseminate that information to the public and disseminate information internally? What was the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: In my sector, information came in from people working in the sector, from all levels, as well as from the Main Staff, and of course from the Defence Department itself and the other sectors there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said "from people working in my sector at all levels." What did you mean by that? Who were those workers of yours, employees, staff from all levels?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: All assistants for IPD at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So they were assistants?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Assistants to the command of the operative zone, the brigade, military assistants, and company assistants.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we're talking about information which was geared towards writing reports or internal information, but did you get reports about the situation, the morale of the units and men in the units, and some extraordinary events? Did you receive information of that kind as well?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And who provided you with that kind of information? How did you come by that information about morale and any extraordinary events and so on? How did that reach you?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Also through two channels; the IPD line and also from the command structure of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber now, please, what the other two sectors did; that is to say, the Administration for Information and Propaganda and Military Psychology? What did the Military Psychology Administration do and the History Administration? Could you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: The Administration for Military Psychology and Personnel Needs, as it was called, was an administration which lacked staff. We didn't have the properly trained military psychologists, not enough of them. But those who were working in that administration had the task of providing services to the soldiers; to assess their level of morale, give them psychological assistance and support, boost morale, test -- they would test the soldiers, and see what morale was like generally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you explain to Their Honours briefly what the Administration for History did, sport, culture and so on?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes. That administration was basically in charge of culture, and within that administration we had a wartime theatre. We also did some publishing work, we had projects in publishing, the area of publishing. It organised sports events, sports/military events, competitions. It amassed archive material and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's go back to the information that you collected and that you received from the chain that you told us about. When it came to informing the public, how did you disseminate that information to the public domain?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: At the very beginning, we did that in writing, statements for the public, daily bulletins, that kind of thing, but soon afterwards the sector started to organise press conferences. And then we would have meetings and discussions with journalists, and then press releases with various comments, interviews and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, once you had collected information you considered to be important, was there anybody in the Defence Department or from the HZ-HB who would authorise what you could make public and what you could not? And I'm talking about the time when you became the assistant in the Defence Department de facto, because you said that you started doing this earlier on, but de facto. Did anybody check the materials and okay or ban any information?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Well, I would have consultation with the head. However, I took over the responsibility of making that decision myself, deciding what to let go and what to keep back, so that's what I did. And I'd like to tell you that as many armies in the war have -- in wars have, the HVO didn't have a censorship department, so I'm conscious of the fact that I took on a great deal of responsibility in that area, but the situation was such that consultations were impossible. It was almost impossible to hold consultations of that nature, so I did the work myself and took on the responsibility myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I'm sorry, I have a question, some clarification. When I hear the witness's testimony, I am told he was the deputy chief of the minister of defence, whereas in English I see "assistant to the head of department." What was he exactly? Was he an assistant, was he a deputy? Were there a lot of deputies and were there a lot of assistants, and which of the two was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was the head of the Department for Information and Propaganda, the IDP, from September 1992 until the 31st of January 1993, and then I was put forward as assistant of the head of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Mindua. I believe there was a mistake in the transcript, because at least the French translation said that "Janvier 1995," but in English it is here "1993." So it is probably a mistake, and it should be "1995." It is what he just mentioned, I believe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The witness said, "The 31st of January, 1993," as it says in the transcript. And as far as his post is concerned, he said that as of the 31st of January, 1993, once again, he was assistant to the head of the Defence Department for IPD, and that has been repeated several times, "assistant to the head of the Defence Department." That was his post as of the 31st of January, 1993. Well, the deputy was another man, and that was Mr. Slobodan Bozic, and we heard him here in court in the capacity of a witness, so he was the deputy, just to make that clear. And if that's clear, maybe we can move on and not waste anymore time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you clarify, please, because Defence counsel has given us the answer. Could you answer, please? Could you answer the question that was put to you by Judge Mindua?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've answered that question. If need be, I will expound on it, I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You can repeat it, Mr. Vegar. Could you please repeat what you were from September 1992, all your posts, until the end of 1993? That period is what we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: From September 1992 until the 31st of January, 1993, I was head of the Administration for Information/Propaganda in the moral upbringing or moral guidance sector, until the 31st of January, 1993. On that date, I was proposed or put forward by the -- Mr. Rajic [as interpreted] to be assistant head of Defence Department for IPD, and I remained there in that post while head of the Defence Department, Mr. Stojic, remained in that post.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, His Honour Mindua asked you a question. Let's clarify it. How many assistants were there in the Defence Department and how many deputies?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: One deputy, Mr. Bozic, and there were several assistants; security assistant or assistant head for security, assistant head for personnel, assistant head for the moral upbringing sector, and assistant head for health issues, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will not insist on bringing up other details. We will see from the documents how it looked like. I would like to go back for a minute --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for interruption, but it's only out of an effort to assist. Back on page 35, on line 24, I believe it was consistent with Mr. Vegar's prior testimony that he was put forward for the new position by Mr. Stojic, not Mr. Rajic, if that's correct, and if we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can continue with you disseminating information. You recently -- in your last answer, you embarked on providing important information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, the question that Mr. Scott posed was heard by the witness and he nodded. It might be good if in the transcript it would be shown that he had nodded, actually, or that he said -- that he answered positively to that question. That's what I perceived. I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are right. I believe that this question was answered at least twice, but let us set the record straight.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who were you proposed to become head of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Head of the department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, put me forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who was occupying that position, assistant head for IPD, before you?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Mr. Bozo Rajic was there before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Once again, when did you receive official appointment, and by whom, to that post? Obviously, there has been some misunderstanding with respect to that question.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Officially, I was appointed on the 27th of August, 1993, by the Croatian Defence Council of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But when did you perform those tasks de facto, those tasks of assistant head to the Defence Department for IPD?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: From the departure of Mr. Rajic from that position, and that was on the 31st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I believe that there are no more misunderstandings about this. Let's go back to what you just recently said. You said that when it came to disseminating the information to the public, you first would consult briefly and then -- for a brief period, and after that brief period you alone determined which information would be disseminated to the public; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that the HVO did not have a censorship department. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what you meant by such a statement?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Military organisations in wartime have usually a censorship department. The HVO, however, did not have such a department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Could you please tell us, from September 1992 and onwards, how often would press conferences be organised, that is, conferences for the press?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Regular press conferences were scheduled for Tuesdays and Fridays, but there were extraordinary conferences as needs arose, and there were some -- such conferences.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How often, from September 1992? Was there a period where they were more frequent or less frequent? Could you give us an impression about the frequency of those press conferences?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Regular press conferences were given by Mr. Bozo Rajic in the autumn of 1992, at the beginning of 1993, when I had already been proposed to take that position. When Mr. Rajic left the post, I took over the task of organising and conducting those press conferences. The regular ones were on Tuesdays and Fridays, but after the security situation in Mostar deteriorated in May and June, those press conferences grew less frequent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: They grew less frequent. Could you tell us about the end of 1993 or the latter part of 1993, how frequent they would be during that period?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Very infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you would organise press conferences, would you invite some guest speakers? Would other people come to attend those press conferences?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes. It was more frequent initially, because this was the only forum to inform the public. Civil service did not do so, so such press conferences would feature people who would be organising humanitarian drive or campaign, or somebody who had published an interesting book, or visitors from abroad and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, were you a sort of spokesman? Who's, if so?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was a spokesman for the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were there any other information departments in the HZ-HB, apart from yours?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: There was. There was the Information Department of the HVO, then the information office of the president of the HZ-HB, and some operations zones had their own information officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The information office of the HVO HZ-HB, did it exist?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you issue press releases or statements for the press, on behalf of the HVO HZ-HB, after the sessions or meetings?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Very rarely. When I would stand in for the person who usually did that, but when he was absent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's be precise. Do you recall the name of the person who was in charge of those tasks in the HVO HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Mr. Drago Maric.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you issue statements to the press on behalf of the Presidency of the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Didn't Mr. Boban ever visit your press conferences as a keynote speaker?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Not a single one that I organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This set of questions concern the information that you disseminated towards the journalists through press conferences. Would such information concern the status of certain battlegrounds that would precede your press conference?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes, the situation on the battle-field, maybe some extraordinary events, casualties that were killed, the dead, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say the killed and the dead, Mr. Vegar. When those press conferences were conducted, you would, beforehand, prepare a report on the information that you had received. Would journalists ask you questions, and what were the issues covered by those questions? Could you answer all those questions or not? Could you please explain to the Trial Bench the practicalities?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Initially, I would state information that I considered relevant. Then I was asked by journalists questions. I would answer everything that I could, which fell within my scope of responsibility and which I had some knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Presiding Judge Antonetti's question was very pertinent, whether you were relaying information as a channel of communication, but I would like you to explain the second question of Judge Antonetti's question. Did you air any political assessment or judgements, and when journalists would ask about politics, what were your answers, and on the basis of which information did you explain your positions on certain political developments?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did answer such questions, among others, about political events or developments, if they concerned the HVO. At that time, such issues were peace conferences, peace negotiations of the parties to the conflict, as they were called, both at the international level and the negotiations and arrangements between local commanders, the armies in conflict, et cetera. Everything that would be of interest of the soldiers or troops or the public, I would disseminate such questions -- issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, we will resume a little later. It's time to have a break now. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, before the break you answered that you would discuss political developments after negotiations, as you said, or -- involving international organisations and negotiations between local commanders. I would like to ask you a precise question. Would you air some political stances about developments that had preceded or peace negotiations that it preceded?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: I did not have the right to do so, and it was not my duty to do so either.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, at those press conferences within your purview, did you engage in propaganda, did you in any way disseminate propaganda or inform the public by way of propaganda, or did you disseminate information that you had collected in the way that you described?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: I did not deal with propaganda. If the information had a propaganda tinge, then that may have been so, but I did not deal with propaganda. Nobody in my sector or department dealt with propaganda. We were not equipped to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's go back to your sector. You explained how the IPD sector was set up. You also said that assistant commanders for IPD existed in military units. Please explain to us what was the relationship between the sector and the assistants for IPD who were in military units, who were in charge of IPD there?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: The relationship was this: I had maintained professional contacts with such people, and they were subordinated to me in terms of the formal links, but they were subordinated to their commanders. There were assistant commanders for IPD, and they were connected to their superior commanders in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you said that you were connected with them through professional links, with those IPD assistants in military units, could you explain to the Chamber what were the professional issues that you dealt with? Did you organise meetings, seminars, training? What were the practical tasks that materialised your links with them?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Whenever we could, we organised meetings, seminars, where we would train and educate IPD operatives. We gave them suggestions, how they were supposed to work from that point onwards. We did so to provide them with more information and to create more cohesion among the members of that sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I did not understand what you said about cohesion of the members of that sector. Are you talking about the sector or assistant commanders for IPD at military unit level?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: I'm talking about all IPD workers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you receive information -- you said that you would collect information for certain press conferences from the Main Staff and the information that was received by the Defence Department about the state of affairs along the battle lines. Did people from the Main Staff provide you with information how it functioned?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Some assistants from brigade level would report to me directly about the situation on the battle-field, about the state -- situation in their military units. The rule was for assistant commander for IPD of operational zones would send to my sector a regular report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this practice according to which individual IPD assistants in brigades send information to you, was that the practice in the entire area, or did some people send you reports more often than others, some people might never said you any reports? Were there any regulations as to how the people sending information to you should act?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Every assistant IPD must first -- was duty-bound to inform his commander, first of all, and then the assistant for IPD at a higher level than his own, and so the information went up the line to the sector. Now, I have to say that some people didn't do their job properly, other people did, and depending on the situation on the battle-ground or in the area of responsibility, they would send out information and reports to the sector and sometimes skip the operative zones.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What I asked you was whether you can remember whether there were any regulations whereby the people working in IPD in the units and the operative zone were required to send their reports to the IPD sector in the Defence Department, for instance.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no, but I think that that was understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, can you tell me, please, when it comes to an assessment -- or, rather, to assess combat readiness through the morale in the units, in your experience, what influenced morale, whether morale was high or low? Was it the events on HZ-HB, events that had negative repercussions on the HVO itself? Did they affect morale? Did you have any knowledge about that and information about that? And if so, did you take any steps to hold information -- informative meetings, or did you perhaps look at the events that influenced the level of morale and so on?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Well, at that time most events influenced morale, because it was a time of great frustration for the soldiers on the battle-front. There was fatigue, numerous losses, so that all this affected the people, the soldiers, and had an effect on morale, all the negative things that they heard about, or that happened, or the rumours going around, or in politics, or in any other area of life, for that matter. So we tried to do our best to prevent morale falling off, and we used our Department for Social Psychology to help us out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting, Ms. Nozica, but sometime and place ago, on page 43, line 11, you asked a question; namely, whether the witness, Mr. Vegar, whether you received information from the General Staff, from the Main Staff, and I think you have not answered this. You have only spoken then of information that came from the brigades directly to you. Did you receive also information from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And am I right to assume, from what you have told us so far, that it would be an IPD person attached to the Main Staff that would give you -- that would be in charge of informing you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Main Staff, I received information from the commander in the Main Staff. Now, while I was the assistant head, we didn't have an assistant for IPD in the Main Staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We'll go back to that question when we come to present documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I asked you about the negative influences on morale with respect to events -- negative events, perhaps soldiers were taken prisoner, the situation with the civilians on the overall HZ-HB area, killings perhaps - I don't want to call them war crimes - but could that have had an especially adverse effect on morale?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Vegar, I'd now like to ask you, once again discussing the subject we're on, to go through some documents, and then on the basis of those documents you'll be able to explain what you've already told us. I think we'll be able to get through them fairly quickly, and I'd like you to have binder 1. Look at document P 1372 first, please, and it should be the first document in your binder. P 1372 is the number. Have you found it? Right. Now, Mr. Vegar, is this a proposal for your appointment as assistant head for IPD of the Defence Department, dated the 31st of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it was sent to the Croatian Defence Council, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and it was signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic; right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Now take a look at the next document, which is P 1374. 1374. And this, once again, is dated the 31st of January, 1993, signed again by Mr. Bruno Stojic, and once again sent to the Croatian Defence Council, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and it is the proposal to relieve of duty, Mr. Rajic, who until then was the assistant head of the department; right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document, which is 2D 00676. And as you say, this is a document about the HVO HZ-HB; right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it appoints you assistant head of the Department of Defence of the Croatian Defence Council, right, and it is dated the 27th of August, 1993; right? And in that same document, we have the fact that Mr. Rajic is relieved of duty, with the same date; right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document, and it is about the establishment of your sector, document P 00586. And I'm going to ask you to take a look at the Croatian version, on page 2, to see what this is about. It is a decision on the basis for establishing the Defence Department, and on the last page of this decision we see that it was put forward by Mr. Mate Boban on the 15th of September, 1992. We've seen this document quite a few times in this courtroom, and it regulates all the sectors that come under the Defence Department, and I'm going to ask you to take a look at paragraph 6 or section 6, where it says: "The assistant head for moral guidance ..." Mr. Vegar, was that another heading, another title that was used at the beginning as the name of your sector?
